articles.title: Faculty and students show how reporting is done when a university partners with local news
articles.author: Teri Finneman, Professor of Journalism, University of Kansas
paras: Catherine Bilskie, the advertising and office manager for the newspaper in Solon, Iowa, had seen many local news outlets close. So she was sure her job at the Solon Economist was about to go one Friday morning in February 2024.

But to her surprise, a new owner, Jason Brummond, appeared. He not only promised to keep her and her co-worker employed at the weekly paper but assured them raises if they agreed to an unusual new venture. And he wasn’t a wealthy benefactor or a representative from a private equity firm – he came from the University of Iowa.

It’s just one example of academic institutions stepping up to address the “news desert” crisis: Thousands of communities across the U.S. have lost local newspapers over the past two decades. And journalism faculty, staff and students are increasingly working together to either rescue legacy newspapers or start new publications for communities lacking local news outlets.

These partnerships have ranged from the Spanish-language news site Noticiero Móvil at the University of Nevada, Reno, to “Good Morning Indian Country” at the University of Kansas, to The Scope at Northeastern in Boston.

We’re journalism professors who have studied and experienced the opportunities and challenges of running community news through higher education. Our new book, “News Desert U,” asks whether this approach is one solution to saving local news. We believe the need is urgent given the stakes and the scope of the crisis.
These experiments come against a grim backdrop.

Over 3,000 newspapers have closed in the U.S. in the past 20 years, including about 170 in 2025, according to Northwestern’s 2026 State of Local News report. Causes include an antiquated business model, declining advertising revenue and hedge-fund buyouts that have gutted papers. Northwestern’s 2025 report estimated that total print newspaper circulation has declined 70% in the past 20 years.
But university partnerships can show promise, we found, with the help of the next generation of journalists.

Iowa’s Solon Economist is one example. The University of Iowa doesn’t actually own the paper, or its sister paper, the Mount Vernon-Lisbon Sun. Still, the relationship is key to making the new venture work.

Its owner, Brummond, is also the publisher of the University of Iowa’s student newspaper, the Daily Iowan, which is owned and operated by the nonprofit Student Publications. While the student newspaper office is inside the journalism school’s building, it operates independently.

In August 2023, Student Publications began talks about buying the Sun and the Economist after the weeklies’ then owner reached out about selling the publications. With both newspapers 20-30 minutes from campus, discussions included how the faculty and students could help the papers.

The Journalism School’s director, Melissa Tully, was immediately in favor – provided that the newspapers’ existing professional staff stay and not be replaced with students. In addition to the editors, this included keeping the advertising and circulation staff.

“They know these communities. So that was really important just from a moral and ethical imperative, but also from a news perspective,” she said. “They’re trusted in their communities. They know what’s going on.”

Student Publications bought both newspapers for US$10,000 in 2024. Since then, circulation has remained stable at both, Brummond said, even as many other publications across the country have suffered declines.
Meanwhile, students in classes such as community news, high school sports, social media marketing and photography contribute for academic credit while other students do paid internships.
Solon Economist Editor Chris Umscheid said he welcomes a revolving door of student interns because it means he’s “actually going to have staff for once.”
“People thought we were going to be the university’s paper, and we’re not,” he said. “I don’t anticipate anything changing there. We’re still going to focus on everything Solon that we can.”

The success has led to Student Publications getting requests to buy other newspapers, Tully said, and it’s working on a list of criteria to consider future partnerships. Brummond cautions these arrangements aren’t easy to pull off, as they require a careful review of finances, workflow and logistical complications that come with a merger.
Liz King, who served as Solon Public Library director, said many locals were afraid the newspaper would close, which would have been a hard blow for the town of about 3,000.
Some readers only get their news through the newspaper, she said. “They’re not comfortable with online sources.”
Dink NeSmith had a similar close scare in Georgia with the The Oglethorpe Echo.

Owner Ralph Maxwell had decided in September 2021 that he had no choice but to shutter the paper due to his own health issues, revenue declines and lack of interest from prospective buyers. He gave NeSmith, an old friend and retired newspaper owner, an early heads-up.
“I don’t know that I want to live in a town that doesn’t have its newspaper,” was NeSmith’s response. He told Maxwell: “You can’t close the Echo.”
NeSmith immediately reached out to the University of Georgia’s journalism school to suggest a partnership.

In the meantime, NeSmith worked to set up a separate nonprofit, Oglethorpe Echo Legacy, for the paper’s new ownership structure. Keeping the newspaper’s finances independent of the university was an important step to ensure the paper would not be subject to any possible “whims” of future administrations, as Charles Davis, the journalism school’s dean, put it. That status was also a signal to Oglethorpe County that the paper’s goal was to serve the community, not make money, he added.
The new nonprofit bought the paper from Maxwell in October 2021 for $10 – a check that Maxwell never cashed and has since been framed.

Davis asked Andy Johnston, an adjunct professor with decades of journalism experience, to serve as the newspaper’s full-time editor. Since November 2021, Johnston has led a team of journalism faculty and students, with the help of several adult staff and volunteers from the county.

The paper covers a wide terrain. Oglethorpe County has over 16,000 people stretching over 442 square miles, and Lexington, where the Echo has its office, is 18 miles (29 kilometers) from the campus in Athens. The reporting staff is provided by journalism professor Amanda Bright’s capstone class – 20 students each semester. Supplementary funding comes from the journalism school, various grants and Echo subscription and advertising funds.

She pairs two students to each beat, with one in charge of a story and the other in charge of editing and producing, with a rotation each week. Students need to turn in eight stories a semester – with corresponding editing and producing assignments that include video, an email newsletter and social media – to get class credit.

When the journalism school took over, the weekly had only a printed newspaper, with no website, social media presence or other digital products, she said. So in their first print edition, the editors outlined their plan for the newspaper to readers and then introduced the student reporters, which they still do every semester.

The partnership has paid off. Print subscriptions to The Echo have doubled and overall digital audience has quadrupled thanks to the launch of new digital products, Bright said. Advertising revenue, meanwhile, has tripled, she said. However, it took some time for local businesses to get used to advertising again, NeSmith said.

But many challenges remain. Johnston has to handle student turnover every semester while students covering events such as government meetings face a steep learning curve and need support. The additional time it takes to edit student copy means content doesn’t appear as quickly. Many faculty members have to work long hours to keep the paper afloat.
But the broader impact is clear: More than two dozen students have gone into local news as a career following their time at the Echo, Bright said.

Should other universities want to follow this model, they need at least two key people in leadership, whether that’s two faculty members or one from faculty and a professional editor, Bright said. “That’s a bottom-line necessity for sanity,” she added.
One common theme from our research is that a service-oriented approach to news that addresses the community’s needs takes priority over profit at these partnerships.

The built-in advantages for these initiatives is that the faculty and staff who tend to manage them get their paychecks and health insurance from their university work. They don’t need to draw a living wage from the news outlet’s finances.

These partnerships are also ideal for students seeking real-world experience while earning class credit or internship wages. And journalism schools are already stocked with multimedia equipment that students can use for their reporting.

Still, they can look deceptively simple on the surface, Brummond said. Tully, at the University of Iowa, recommends other interested universities should go slowly. Building a successful project takes patient experimentation and a willingness to regroup when needed, in her view.
“Doing this slowly is OK,” she said. “In the end, it’s going to be better. So far, that’s been a good recipe for us.”
Teri Finneman and Pamela Walck are co-authors of the book "News Desert U."

Pamela E. Walck does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: School librarians are vanishing from Michigan schools just when they are needed most
articles.author: Shannon Oltmann, Associate Dean of Information Sciences, Wayne State University
paras: Fewer than 10% of Michigan public schools report having a school library staffed with a trained school librarian.

Although Michigan strongly recommends that schools employ certified librarians, the state does not require them. In the 2023–24 school year, the state ranked 46th in the student-to-librarian ratio, with one school librarian for every 2,760 students.

The lack of school librarians impacts students across Michigan, but particularly in low-income communities like Detroit and Flint and more isolated ones like Alcona County in the northern Lower Peninsula and Ontonagon in the Upper Peninsula, exacerbating disparities in resources for young people.

We are scholars in library and information sciences from Wayne State University, studying information access and ethics and equity in education and school libraries. Currently, we are conducting a statewide campaign to contact every school in Michigan and learn about their libraries, staffing, book collections, technology resources and more.

Michigan’s 2025–26 School Aid budget funded our statewide survey to measure the school librarian shortage and guide efforts to address it. Our work, and the work of many others, reveals how school librarians help students become strong readers and informed citizens.
Catalysts for student achievement

A missing librarian is harder to see than an empty bookshelf. A room full of books can look like a school library. But if students cannot borrow those books, teachers have no librarian to plan lessons with, and no one leads author visits or digital citizenship lessons, the space offers only a fraction of what a school library can provide.

School librarians bring those services to life. Also called school library media specialists, they hold a teaching certificate and complete advanced education. They connect students with books they want to read and work with teachers to build richer lessons, using library resources to extend learning beyond the textbook.

Their impact stretches far beyond standardized test scores, though studies link strong library programs with higher student achievement and improved student literacy, especially for struggling readers. They can instill a love of reading and teach technological skills, which is critical in the age of artificial intelligence.

At our Michigan School Census symposium held in 2026, Michigan school librarians and a principal described what that work looks like. Brian Peck, a teacher librarian at Detroit’s UPrep Academy, helped students research and build a library where none had existed. He reported that 334 students voluntarily visited and checked out books during the previous school year.

At West Ottawa, librarian Julia Reynolds described replacing crowded shelves with displays that let children see book covers. Circulation quadrupled, she reported. A principal on the panel explained how district support helped schools make library visits a priority from the first week of school.
Students’ information worlds
Access to information is only a start. Students also need help making sense of what reaches them through searches, social media and AI.
AI can create convincing fake videos of students doing or saying things they never did, harming their reputations and undermining trust in what people see online.

Less visible forces shape students’ information worlds, too. Algorithms and online platforms often dictate which search results and suggested videos appear first. Students need to understand that the first result is not necessarily the most credible or trustworthy source. AI is becoming so prominent that even elementary school students are learning about it.
Building information literacy
Information literacy means knowing how to find, judge and use information. School librarians turn those skills into practice.
For a history assignment, a librarian might help students compare a newspaper account with a firsthand record. Who produced each source? What might explain their different accounts?
The same habits apply to AI. Students can trace a claim to its source, check whether the source exists and compare what it says with the generated answer. A confident response still needs evidence.

Guided by certified school librarians, students can build upon these foundations and learn to effectively find, evaluate and use information, including news articles about a historic event for a social studies assignment or to analyze current social media trends. Students can also judge the accuracy, recency and relevance of information. They learn to apply information in decision-making, writing and other forms of communication.
Becoming savvy digital citizens
Knowing whether information is trustworthy is an important skill. Deciding what to do with it is another.
Digital citizenship includes deciding whether to post someone’s photo, seeking their permission before doing so, and choosing not to share a fake video.
Recent research emphasizes that digital citizenship prepares students to be empowered online and act ethically, safely and legally in digital environments.
Our work also starts with the knowledge young people bring to school.

Project Restoring Urban School Libraries helped classroom teachers earn the additional endorsement needed to become school librarians. The program combined mentoring with coursework that drew on students’ cultures, including using hip-hop to explore how young people find, create and share information.
Students start by examining the media they already use. A lesson might ask them to trace a sample, credit its creator and discuss what changes when someone else’s work reaches a new audience.

Principal preparation programs can help school leaders understand what school librarians contribute beyond book checkout. But principals and school librarians often train in separate academic units: colleges of education and schools of library and information science. Without shared coursework or joint projects, principals may complete their training without learning how to work with a school librarian.

In our “Closing the Literacy Gap” symposium, we brought school librarians and administrators together on a panel to show what their partnerships make possible. West Ottawa Principal Audra Bolhuis joined school librarian Julia Reynolds and compared a librarian to “an instructional coach.” She described someone teachers can turn to for resources and help with classroom projects, extending the librarian’s role beyond students’ scheduled library visits.
School library jobs remain vulnerable to budget cuts, and the number of school librarians across the state has been decreasing since 2010.

To understand what schools provide and where support is missing, we launched the state-funded Michigan School Census in September 2026. By Oct. 21, 1,054 schools – about one-third of those invited – had completed it. Our public response map tracks participation across districts.

Schools without libraries or librarians are essential to painting the full picture: Their staff can explain how students get books and research help when those services are absent. The findings will guide recommendations for staffing, resources and funding.
Counting what schools have is the first step toward deciding what every Michigan student should be able to count on.

I am Associate Dean/Director of the School of Information Sciences at Wayne State University, which received an appropriation from the Michigan Legislature in 2025. The funding was routed through the Michigan Department of Education, to Wayne State University, then to my School. I do not benefit directly from funding (i.e., no income). Second, I am a recipient of a current National Leadership Grant from the Institute of Museum and Library Services, for $445,000. This grant funds research to study how public libraries respond to censorship.

articles.title: Spending in-person time with friends is the biggest predictor of whether college students flourish
articles.author: Roxanne Prichard, Professor of Psychology, University of St. Thomas
paras: Exercise, avoiding alcohol or even getting enough sleep aren’t the factors most connected to college students’ well-being.

Spending face-to-face time with friends and other people is the strongest predictor of their mental health, according to a 2026 study of nearly 80,000 students that I conducted with the help of my students.
This finding matters because young people are spending less time together in person and more time communicating through screens.
Between 2010 and 2022, the percentage of U.S. high school seniors who reported seeing friends face-to-face almost every day declined from 44% to 32%.
Against this backdrop, mental health challenges among young people have become an increasing public health concern.
Suicide remains the second-leading cause of death among Americans ages 15 to 34.
But mental health is about more than the absence of mental illness. My student researchers and I wanted to ask a somewhat different question: What helps young people flourish?

To answer that question, we created a broad measure of well-being that captured more than the lack of mental health problems, such as psychological distress. It also included positive aspects of life, such as having supportive relationships, hobbies and a sense of meaning and purpose.
A range of measures to determine well-being
Our research team analyzed responses from 79,246 college students across the United States and Canada.
We examined 51 aspects of students’ lives, including their substance use, the discrimination they encountered, their financial stress, any sleep problems and different relationship challenges.
We also examined how students spent their free time, whether that meant exercising, studying, socializing, meditating, playing video games or scrolling on social media.

We used statistical methods that allowed us to compare dozens of potential influences on student well-being simultaneously, helping us identify which factors were most strongly associated with flourishing.
Among the dozens of factors we examined, six stood out as the most important and influential.
Time spent with others pays off

The strongest factor connected to student flourishing was remarkably ordinary: spending time with other people. Students who spent more hours socializing with friends, attending student organizations and participating in cultural events tended to report feeling an overall sense of well-being.

The second most important factor surprised us. Students who spent more time on obligations, including paid work and unpaid family responsibilities, also tended to report a greater sense of well-being.
Our results raise an intriguing possibility: Well-being may come not only from leisure and self-care but also from contributing to something larger than oneself.

While problematic substance use, passive screen time and sleep problems tended to compromise well-being, these factors weren’t the biggest detriment. It was difficulty navigating interpersonal relationships, including problems with friends, romantic partners and roommates.
Making friends, maintaining healthy relationships and working through conflicts requires practice, and some of that practice time now competes with communication mediated by screens.

Notably, the contributors to student flourishing were similar among students diagnosed with anxiety or depression and those without these diagnoses. That suggests these everyday experiences may matter across a broad spectrum of mental health.

Supporting students’ mental and emotional health is not simply a matter of reducing screen time. It also means making it easier for young people to spend time together in person, whether through clubs, recreation programs, community events or other welcoming spaces.
Counseling and educational programs can likewise help students build friendships, communicate effectively and navigate conflict in healthy ways.

None of this means mental illness can be solved by telling a struggling young person to put down their phone, join a club or get more sleep. Mental health conditions are complex, and people experiencing them need access to effective professional care.

But our findings suggest that helping young people thrive requires more than treating symptoms. It also requires cultivating supportive relationships, healthy sleep and meaningful engagement in work, school and family life.
Roxanne Prichard receives funding from the National Science Foundation.

articles.title: Boo! How to pick scary books for kids that thrill but won’t haunt for life
articles.author: Liz Rosenberg, Professor of English, General Literature and Rhetoric, Binghamton University, State University of New York
paras: Halloween is one of the few holidays centered around children. When else can students come to school dressed like astronauts, monsters and witches, or ring strangers’ doorbells to ask for candy?
But of course there’s a darker side to the holiday.

Horror’s bloody images lurk in the shadows – from ghouls leering over people’s lawns to skeletons hanging from trees – whether invited or not. Thoughtful adults might wonder, what is the right amount of scary for a child?
As a professor of children’s literature, and a writer of children’s books, I turn to the great author and illustrator Maurice Sendak for a hint.

A child’s mother once told Sendak that her pre-schooler was terrified of his classic 1963 book “Where the Wild Things Are,” which brings the reader into the world of an imaginative child, Max, after his mother sends him to his room without dinner. Through his imagination, Max journeys to a world of fantastical creatures called Wild Things.
No matter how many times this mother read “Where the Wild Things Are” to her young child, he screamed.
“What are you, a sadist?” Sendak answered. “Read him something else.”
“Why,” he continued, “would any one book be right for every child?”

When considering the benefits and drawbacks of scary books to get in the spirit of Halloween, some possible choices come to mind, along with some reminders to both overly cautious and sometimes careless adults.
Facing your jitters head on

To start, Felicia Bond’s 1987 “The Halloween Performance,” later republished as “The Halloween Play,” is a perfect Halloween picture-book classic, appealing to all ages and offering humor and suspense.
Bond is the illustrator of the 1985 children’s best seller, “If You Give a Mouse a Cookie,” and subsequent books. An adorable young mouse features in this Halloween story, as well.
The plot revolves around a mysterious “small but important part” that Roger, a nervous, brown mouse, has landed in the school Halloween performance.
Costumed skeletons and witches don’t bother him – but his jitters about performing on stage do.
Roger overcomes stage-fright to shine in the school performance. He may inspire other children to overcome their own feelings of nervousness at Halloween and make fun memories.
Frog and Toad show that fear can be fun
Frog and Toad are Arnold Lobel’s beloved, amphibian best friends from his children’s series published in the 1970s.

Though they have very different personalities, both Frog and Toad enjoy the thrill of playing with fear. In “Shivers,” a story in the book “Days with Frog and Toad,” Frog tells Toad a tale about “the old dark Frog” who combs the woods in search of tasty children.
Toad keeps asking, “Is this real?” Frog answers like any good storyteller, “Maybe it is and maybe it isn’t.”
Together the duo enjoy scaring themselves into a teeth-chattering but delightful evening.
They show young readers that, in the right doses, fear can be fun: ask any kid scream-laughing on a roller-coaster.
In another story, “Dragons and Giants,” Frog and Toad test their own heroism after reading fairy tales about dragons and giants.
“The people in this book are brave,” said Toad. “They fight dragons and giants, and they are never afraid.”
“I wonder if we are brave,” said Frog. Frog and Toad looked into a mirror. “We look brave,” said Frog. “Yes, but are we?” asked Toad.
Frog and Toad are both fearful and brave, as most of us are.

Wise children’s stories reinforce the truth that it’s natural to be both, sometimes at the same time. “Frog and Toad” features color illustrations in subtle greens and browns, leaving enough space for kids to imagine new facets of themselves – the timid and the bold.
Scary stories can be a natural part of childhood
Fear is inevitably woven into the fabric of children’s lives.
Nightmares, for example, spring from unknown sources, though studies show they are intensified by trauma, emotional disturbances and exposure to violence.
Bad dreams – like scary stories – work as fire drills for the developing brain.

“Bad dreams may even provide evolutionary protection for the young, by allowing children to practice bravery while they are safely at home and in bed,” writes Dierdre Barrett, editor of the book “Traumas and Dreams.” She notes that children are smaller and more “vulnerable to many more threats than adults. Nightmares … reflect this vulnerability.”
Recognizing the difference between fantasy and reality is a form of practicing fear management – which strengthens resilience and resistance.
Maybe that’s why some older elementary school kids actively seek out frightening reading.

When written well and thoughtfully, such books provide more delight than dismay. The only hair-raising thing about Alvin Schwartz’s “Scary Stories” is Stephen Gammell’s high-contrast, dreamlike art. Schwartz, a writer and folklorist, gathered spooky tales from all over the United States and compiled them into three of the most popular children’s books of the 1980s.

While Schwartz retells classic folklore tales with humor and goosebumps in equal measure, Gammell’s powerful drawings nudge children wordlessly toward the ghoulish. It’s a good match: The three-book series has proven irresistible to young readers for 40 years.
At the darkest haunting edge of the children’s horror genre, books like Roald Dahl’s “The Witches” totter between imaginatively eerie and terror-producing.
In this book, ordinary-seeming women unmask themselves as grotesquely evil witches. Their goal is to capture human children, transforming them into mice that they will trap and kill.
Navigating scary things, safely

What constitutes protection and when does it deny the child a chance to explore their fears? I believe we want our children to enjoy adventures, to test themselves and discover inner courage when they least expect it.
We also don’t want them to be haunted for life. The right books for the right child at the right time can help children and adults safely navigate those waters.
I wrote the book “Monster Mama,” with pictures by Stephen Gammell, who also illustrated the “Scary Stories” series.

articles.title: State takeovers of struggling Texas school districts come at a high cost, with little evidence of success
articles.author: Daniel H. Robinson, Professor, College of Education, University of Texas at Arlington
paras: Local school boards and district administrators typically determine how public schools are run. If students are not meeting basic academic standards, though, state governments sometimes step in and take over the day-to-day operations of entire school districts.
Since 1989, state officials have been appointed to temporarily replace elected school boards and superintendents in more than 100 districts across at least 22 states.

Texas has used takeovers more than most. Since 2015, the state has temporarily stepped in to run eight districts. A Texas law allows the state to take over for at least two years if one or more schools within the district has poor academic performance for five consecutive years.
Fourteen additional districts in Texas are now at risk of a takeover.
As an education professor at the University of Texas at Arlington, I often evaluate educational policies and interventions.

As part of this work, I teach a class on evaluating evidence for whether initiatives live up to their claims. Based on my research, Texas taking over school districts is not always helping the students there.
A decade of Texas school takeovers
When a state takeover occurs, the state appoints a replacement school board, rather than holding an election. It also appoints a superintendent instead of allowing the district to hire one.

In October 2025, the Texas Education Agency announced that it was appointing a new school board and superintendent for Fort Worth Independent School District, one of the largest school districts in Texas.
Approximately 82% of students in this district live in poverty.

Marissa Sanchez, a mother with three children in Fort Worth public schools, told local station NBC 5 in October 2025, “these people that don’t know our communities, don’t know our students, what kind of representation will they bring, because we will no longer have a say in our local representative decision-making.”
Fort Worth’s school district had over 1,000 teachers announce their resignation during the 2025-26 school year after the announced state takeover – up 58% from the previous year.
It costs between US$11,000 to $20,000 for every new teacher to be recruited, trained and put in the classroom. That does not include salary, health insurance or other standard employment benefits.
State-run school districts skew poor, minority

Only 12% of Texas schools with 80% to 100% of the student population living in poverty achieved an A performance grade during the 2024-2025 school year. Meanwhile, 67% of Texas schools with a 0% to 20% poverty rate achieved an A grade, according to the Texas Education Agency.

Similarly, while 6% of students at schools with a majority-Black student population earned A’s, 16% of students at Hispanic-majority schools earned A’s. This compares with 35% of students at majority-white schools who received A’s.
At the eight Texas districts that the state has taken over – and the 14 currently at risk for a takeover – more than half of students who attend are eligible for free or reduced lunch.

And at the large districts that have been taken over, such as Houston and Fort Worth, more than 8 out of 10 students live in low-income households. A majority of students there are Black and Hispanic.
Negative effect on enrollment and staffing
When states take over school districts, student enrollment typically declines. Staff turnover, meanwhile, increases.

Teacher attrition – meaning teachers who left the profession – increased by 48% during the first two years after the 2023 Houston takeover compared with the five years before. Almost 5,000 teachers left during the first year of the takeover, and another 3,300 left in the second year.
Principal turnover also increased dramatically in Houston, with 177 changes across 274 schools since 2024.

In 2023-2024, less than a year after the takeover, Houston had over 1,000 teachers not certified to teach. A year later, it had over 2,000 uncertified teachers because of a state law that allows teachers to waive the requirement that all teachers are licensed in certain cases.

Since the start of the takeover, about 21,000 fewer students will attend Houston public schools in 2026-2027, costing the district about $190 million in state funding. Many of these students are simply attending nearby schools that are not part of Houston Independent School District.
Takeovers work, according to Texas Education Commissioner Mike Morath.
“In every single intervention, the results were higher, or at least no worse after the board of managers was placed than before,” Morath told the Fort Worth Report in September 2025.
But national evidence suggests otherwise.

A recent study of school takeovers nationwide concluded that takeovers, on average, do not improve student achievement. Rather, they are usually immediately disruptive to students’ reading achievement.

University of Texas at Arlington graduate students Veronica Erives, Nasja Aude, Jaclyn Foster and Cole Davis and I examined two Texas school districts, Shepherd and Marlin, in the spring of 2026, in forthcoming research.
Uneven results after the takeover

Marlin Intermediate School District, a small-town district in central Texas, has about 800 students, 99% of whom live below the poverty level. Approximately 61% of the students there are Black, 31% Hispanic and 6% white.

The state took over Marlin schools in 2017, following five consecutive years of failing performance grades. In 2019, Morath extended state oversight of Marlin following continued low academic performance.

At the time of its takeover a few years later, in 2020, Shepherd Intermediate School District served approximately 2,000 students across four rural campuses in southeast Texas, with 71% of students considered economically disadvantaged.
The district’s student population was approximately 56% white and 35% Hispanic, making it one of the few predominantly white districts in Texas to experience a state takeover.
In both Shepherd and Marlin, teacher turnover continues to be a problem years after the takeover.
Comparing year-to-year performance at these districts is difficult, due to a redesign of the state’s standardized testing program in the 2022–2023 school year.
The Texas Education Agency explicitly notes that scores from 2023 onward cannot be directly compared to older test data.
There is a way, however, to sort of standardize the “approach grade level” percentages by comparing them to the state percentages. This has the effect of controlling for yearly changes in the tests.

For Marlin, my analysis shows, the percentage of third graders who approached grade level for reading in 2016 – one year prior to the state takeover – was 41%. This compares with 73% of third graders in Texas who were reading at this level in 2016. For third grade math, Marlin’s score in 2016 was 29%, compared with 75% for the state that year.

By 2019, two years into the takeover, 44% of third graders were approaching their grade level for reading, and 51% of them were doing the same for math, compared with the state averages of 78% on reading and 78% on math.

And in 2025, while 55% of third graders in Marlin schools were reading at grade level, just 40% were completing math questions at grade level. This compared with the state’s 74% and 74% averages that year, respectively. So, slight improvement in reading, none in math, and still way below the state averages.

For Shepherd, 56% of third graders approached grade level for reading in 2018, one year prior to the state takeover. This compared with the state average of 77%. For third grade math, 57% of Shepherd students were approaching grade level, compared with the state’s 78% average in 2018.
By 2025, the percentages for third grade reading and math were 56 and 50, compared with the state’s 77 and 71, respectively. No gains to speak of.
Similar trends exist for seventh grade reading and math.

Our study shows little evidence of student achievement improvements to support takeovers. When weighed against the costs of declining enrollments, teacher and principal turnover, and monetary costs, one has to ask if takeovers are worth it.

Daniel H. Robinson does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Students take up to 88 standardized tests before high school, but more testing doesn’t improve learning
articles.author: Liza Bondurant, Associate Professor of Secondary Math Education, Mississippi State University
paras: The public K-12 school system in the United States has become pervasively shaped by standardized testing.
I began teaching mathematics in 2005, four years after the federal law No Child Left Behind was enacted. This law expanded state testing and tied test results to school performance.
Most districts changed their curricula to focus more on the content and skills covered on state tests.
Many school districts increased their instructional weekly time for English and mathematics, with average increases of 47% for English and 37% for mathematics from 2001 to 2007.
To make room for additional time spent on these subjects, 44% of school districts cut time from other subjects or activities, such as the arts.
A 2026 study of 67 school districts across 38 states found that, before high school, students take a median of 57 state- and district-required assessments.
A short-lived law with lasting effects
No Child Left Behind was replaced by another law, the Every Student Succeeds Act, in 2015.

Although the Every Student Succeeds Act aimed to reduce the role of testing in classrooms, standardized tests continue to shape what teachers teach, how they use instructional time and how schools define success.

All U.S. public schools are required to administer standardized tests in reading and math annually to students in grades three through eight and at least once in high school. These tests measure whether students are reading and understanding mathematics at, above or below the average, when compared to other students across the state.
Students’ scores on these tests can affect schools’ ratings and rankings, and can also determine whether states monitor or take over public school districts that are not performing well.

The exact number of tests students take each year before high school ranges from 35 to 88 tests. The study also found no relationship between the number of assessments students took and their proficiency or growth in English or mathematics.
The National Association of State Boards of Education also reports that some districts give students seven assessments per grade, with most tests administered one to three times a year.
Older research also documents the time teachers spend preparing students for state tests.

A 2016 survey found that 62% of K-12 public school teachers reported spending too much time preparing students for state-mandated tests. Teachers estimated spending an average of 14 out of 180 school days preparing students for these exams, whether it be reviewing the question formats students see on tests or teaching test-taking strategies.
In the same 2016 national survey, 29% of teachers reported spending more than a month preparing students in grades K-12 for state-mandated tests.
Teachers also feel the effects of spending so much time preparing students for standardized tests.
Research on teacher turnover has found that teachers’ dissatisfaction with standardized testing was a key reason they left the profession.
Other research from 2026 found that teachers who worried about job consequences tied to test results reported lower job satisfaction.
These numbers tell a larger story. The costs of standardized testing do not simply appear in the amount printed on contracts with testing companies.

They are also reflected in lesson plans, teachers’ workloads, classroom time, professional autonomy and the opportunities that disappear when preparing for a test becomes a central purpose of schooling.

A test can measure learning. But when some students take as many as 88 assessments before high school and teachers report spending weeks preparing students for state exams, it’s important to ask whether it’s the best use of their limited time.

I work in Mississippi, where many communities are rural and agriculture is a major industry. Recently, I lamented to a local farmer about the time and money spent on standardized testing. He offered a simple response: “You don’t get a pig to grow by measuring it more.” His words capture the question at the heart of this debate: Does more testing help students learn, or does it take time away from learning?

articles.title: Do you think teachers are similar to coaches, pastors or something else? It depends on where you live
articles.author: Gustavo E. Fischman, Professor of Education Policies and Comparative Studies, Arizona State University
paras: Three answers, three countries, one open-ended question: “Teaching is similar to what other occupation or activity?”
We asked this question to more than 3,000 people across the United States, England and Australia between May 2025 and March 2026.
Coaching was the front-runner across all three countries. But the similarities partially diverged there.

Respondents in England and Australia more often compared teaching with professional roles such as nursing and social work. U.S. respondents, meanwhile, more often likened teaching to being a parent and religious roles, such as a cleric or pastor.
In the three countries, however, one other idea stood out: Teaching was primarily associated with a caring relationship.
We have previously examined how Republicans and Democrats in the U.S. find common ground on what makes a good teacher, despite the polarization in the country on education and many other issues.
This time, we wanted to know whether people across countries had similar ideas of teachers.

In all three countries, respondents most often described teaching as centered in the relationship between teacher and student: a form of coaching, caregiving, parenting and other types of personal support.
Coaching was the most common answer in each country, but its prominence varied.
Coaching was named by 30% of U.S. respondents, compared with 23% in England and 23% in Australia.
The differences became more pronounced when participants named other occupations and activities.
Respondents in England and Australia were more likely to associate teaching with institutional, credentialed and paid professional roles, such as nursing, lecturing and social work.

“Nursing. They care for and look after people whilst they are at their most vulnerable. Teachers do a similar thing by caring and teaching young people some of the skills they will need later in life,” a 39-year-old Australian man told us.
“A lecturer, you are passing on knowledge to people, usually the younger generation,” another 32-year-old man in England said.

Compared with respondents in those countries, U.S. respondents were more likely to describe teaching through caregiving roles, such as parenting, and through religious figures, such as priests, pastors or rabbis.
“Being a parent, you are caring for young minds and shaping them through learning,” a 33-year-old woman in the U.S. told us.
“As a preacher, he teaches the word of God. How they deliver the word determines how well the people will understand it,” a 23-year-old woman in the U.S. said.

While international comparisons are informative, they do not represent a single view of teaching. Instead, they suggest that respondents in three countries likely drew on somewhat different cultural repertoires when describing the profession.
We were surprised by just how much agreement we found.

Despite differences in schooling models and cultural norms, people in the United States, England and Australia had remarkably similar ideas about how relationships are at the heart of teaching, closely echoing our other work showing that Republicans and Democrats view teachers similarly.
AI is not at the center of people’s thinking
In September 2026, The New York Times conducted an informal survey of 37 education researchers who gave 30 ideas about how to fix schools.

Their list consists primarily of interventions such as more per-pupil funding, banning cellphones and restricting artificial intelligence in the classroom. These ideas appeared far less often in our participants’ explanations of what teaching resembles.
In fact, out of more than 3,000 responses to our survey, AI came up only a handful of times and never as the reason teaching and another occupation were said to be alike.
Given how central AI has become to political and academic debates about the future of education, its near-total absence in these public descriptions of teaching is notable.
At the same time, experts and citizens agree that what separates very good teaching from poor execution is likely the quality of the relationship between educators and children.

We think that serious conversation about student achievement must include clear descriptions of very good teachers: the practices they use to encourage and enable students to learn. Our research shows that teaching should make room for both the transmission of knowledge and the meaningful and caring relationships that make learning possible.

articles.title: What colleges and universities need from donors to thrive
articles.author: William Blomquist, Professor Emeritus of Political Science, Indiana University
paras: In 1638, John Harvard, an English-born Puritan minister and teacher in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, bequeathed 400 books and half his £779 estate, today equivalent to roughly US$2 million, to the college that would be renamed in his honor after his death.

In addition to launching America’s oldest university, Harvard’s donation began a tradition of philanthropy for U.S. colleges and universities that has continued ever since. Today, philanthropy is an important source of higher education funding that covers an average of 10% of college and university budgets.

Based on our decades of experience as scholars, academic administrators and school fundraisers, we believe that donors – and not just big ones – are especially important to colleges and universities in tough times.

Since January 2025, the Trump administration has targeted colleges and universities with research funding cuts, student financial aid caps and new restrictions on how long international students can stay in the United States.

University endowments have been in the crosshairs since the first Trump administration’s 2017 tax reform package. The big 2025 tax-and-spending package Trump signed raised the taxes on some schools’ endowments. A rule the Trump administration proposed in September 2026 would threaten private schools’ tax-exempt status if any of their programs use race-based criteria.
There are demographic problems too. Fewer students are choosing to go to college, and the number of high school graduates who could attend is falling due to a declining birthrate.
Although colleges and universities are providing more financial aid than ever, students and their families are still struggling to pay for college.

Some schools are being forced to close their doors. Sixteen colleges shut down in 2025 alone, including Indiana’s only predominantly Black college, Martin University, and ecologically focused Sterling College in Vermont.
And at least 40 colleges have been acquired by other schools since 2020, including Marymount Manhattan College and Mills College, which are now part of Northeastern University’s global network.
Donors contributed $79 billion to colleges and universities in 2025, up 4% in constant dollars from the year before.
The richest Americans dominate giving to higher education: 89% of the funds raised came from only 2% of donors in 2025.

Also in 2025, Phil and Penny Knight, the Nike co-founder and his wife, made what was then the largest single gift to a university in history when they gave the Oregon Health & Science University $2 billion for cancer research.
On Sept. 30, 2026, investor Ken Griffin broke that record by giving Carnegie Mellon University more than $3 billion to build a new campus in Miami and meet some other priorities.

It’s hardly the only megagift a university has received in 2026: Michael and Susan Dell, whose fortune comes from his computer hardware company, gave the University of Texas at Austin $750 million for its medical center. The Knights gave $1 billion to the University of Oregon for a new engineering college. Software billionaire David Duffield pledged $371 million to Cornell University. And many other schools have drawn gifts in excess of $100 million.

The vast majority of these huge gifts are reserved for specific purposes. The share of totally unrestricted gifts to colleges and universities, those given with no strings attached, has been dwindling for decades. In 2024 it slipped below 7%. Unrestricted giving did pick up somewhat in 2025. Perhaps that was a sign that some donors were responding to federal funding cuts with their gifts.

In an article in Change: The Magazine of Higher Learning in September 2026, we listed ideas for college and university fundraising efforts. These tie to three recommendations for donors – and not only those making multimillion-dollar gifts.
Donations to colleges and universities don’t have to end in lots of zeros to make a big difference.

In 2015, the grassroots Saving Sweet Briar campaign kept the small women’s college operating even after its trustees had voted to close it. The largest gift the rural Virginia school received was $2 million, and the smallest was $1.50 from a graduate’s grandchild. This is the exception rather than the rule. Financial pressures were too much for Hampshire College, a New England private college that is slated to close after the fall semester of 2026, to withstand – even with a fundraising campaign and $5 million gift from alum and documentary filmmaker Ken Burns.

Giving Days are high-profile fundraising campaigns through which many alumni and other supporters raise millions. For example, Oregon State University Dam Proud Day 2026 drew 12,400 gifts and raised over $4.1 million. Purdue University’s annual “day of giving” has generated nearly $500 million over the past decade. In 2024, it garnered $76 million from 32,000 donors.
2. Donating with few or no strings attached
Donations with few restrictions or none at all help colleges and universities meet their greatest needs.
Even if they’re mostly intended for a new building or to fund a particular program, large gifts can also include unrestricted portions to help cover costs as needs arise and priorities change.

Brandeis University, Indiana University, Princeton University and other schools encourage unrestricted annual gifts. These flexible funds are helping to cover research funding shortfalls at Cornell University, undergraduate scholarships at Georgetown University and general operations at the College of the Atlantic.

Novelist and philanthropist MacKenzie Scott, the former wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, has given more than $26 billion in unrestricted donations to nonprofits, including to colleges and universities. Historically Black colleges and universities as well as other schools with diverse student bodies, such as Robeson Community College in rural North Carolina, Oklahoma’s Carl Albert State College and Wisconsin’s Fond du Lac Tribal and Community College, have received Scott’s big gifts.

In 1920, the trustees of Berea College, a private liberal arts school in Kentucky, passed a resolution placing future unrestricted bequests, donations made through people’s estates, in the school’s endowment. Berea students do not pay for tuition, fees, housing or food – thanks in large part to those unrestricted donations.
3. Helping students afford all college costs so they can graduate
Supporting students directly helps them go to college, stay in school and graduate.

Donors already make gifts that fund schools’ financial aid packages, with about $7 billion in gifts designated for this purpose in 2025. But the colleges and universities that receive the most dollars from donors serve a small fraction of the nation’s undergraduate students – and not those from low-income families. We recommend that donors consider making gifts to the thousands of colleges and universities, including community colleges, that don’t typically draw big donations and have endowments totaling in the millions, rather than billions, of dollars.

Sometimes it takes more than tuition scholarships for students to graduate. Donors can pay for additional expenses, such as transportation and textbooks, and fund extra academic advising and mentoring. Billionaire philanthropists John and Laura Arnold’s Commit2Completion grant program at Arizona’s Maricopa Community Colleges addresses those kinds of often overlooked priorities.

You don’t have to be very wealthy to fund scholarships. Anyone can pitch in through platforms like Dollars for Scholars. This program’s more than 400 chapters enable local donors to pool their gifts to help students raised in their communities pay college expenses. For example, a rural Minnesota chapter awarded $248,000 to 65 college-bound students in 2025.

There are also hundreds of other place-based “promise programs” that provide tuition and fees scholarships to public colleges and universities in their areas and offer programming such as college readiness workshops and access to local employers.

Philanthropy can’t solve every problem higher education faces. But by giving together, donating with fewer strings attached and helping students pay their college expenses, alumni and other donors can be strategic in how they help.
Genevieve Shaker has received funding from the TIAA Institute and the AFP Foundation for Philanthropy.

articles.title: Why faculty diversity at universities still lags far behind the changing demographics of college students
articles.author: Rodney Coates, Professor of Critical Race and Ethnic Studies, Miami University
paras: U.S. colleges and universities have long struggled to increase the racial diversity of their faculty.

And after they are hired, some faculty of color say they feel that their qualifications and scholarship are subjected to greater scrutiny, or that they do not feel valued by their colleagues and schools.

As a scholar of critical race theory, I have studied these barriers, and I think that it is helpful to understand what universities, students and academic research all stand to gain from a more diverse faculty.
While college faculties have become more racially diverse since the 1970s, the diversification of the faculty has not kept pace with changes in the college student population.
Overall, approximately 16% of the U.S. population were of color in 1970.
In 1975, approximately 8% of full-time faculty at U.S. colleges and universities were people of color. Approximately 4% were Black, 2% were Asian, and 1% were Hispanic.
In 1976, meanwhile, nearly 16% of U.S. college students were people of color.
Black students specifically accounted for about 9% of all full-time college students in 1976, Hispanic students about 4% and Asian or Pacific Islander students about 2%.

By 2022, 72% of full-time faculty across universities and colleges nationwide were white, while Asian professors made up 13%, Black professors 7% and Hispanic professors 6%, according to the National Center for Education Statistics.
By 2022, Hispanic students accounted for 21.5% of U.S.-resident students at colleges and universities, Black students 13.2% and Asian students 7.8%.
Overall, in 2022, people of color made up approximately 41% of the U.S. population.
Diversifying college faculties has not been a straightforward journey in recent years.
After a white police officer shot and killed Michael Brown, a Black teenager living in Ferguson, Missouri, in 2014, student protests erupted across college campuses.
Amid this student activism around racism, some U.S. research universities publicly committed to making their faculties more diverse.
By 2015, at least 88 of the country’s 187 leading research universities had promised to take this step.
Another 96 schools made similar commitments over the next few years, including after the 2020 police murder of George Floyd, a Black man living in Minneapolis.
Among a group of selected research universities examined by The Washington Post, the share of Black, Hispanic and other underrepresented faculty rose from 9% in 2015 to 12% in 2024.

But many of those public efforts have since been scaled back or abandoned. Of the 184 universities that had made faculty-diversity commitments, at least 108 had fully or partially rolled them back by early 2026.

Separately, in 2023, more than 45 bills meant to restrict or ban diversity, equity and inclusion efforts in higher education were introduced in state legislatures. By late that year, eight states had enacted anti-DEI laws.
These measures have included restrictions on schools’ DEI offices and programs, diversity statements and spending on DEI-related initiatives.
Some scholars argue that these policies, along with other restrictions on racial-equity programs and initiatives, are contributing to what they describe as the “resegregation” of higher education.

Some faculty of color have said that they have seen evidence of a kind of tokenism in higher education. Some feel that they are expected to represent, exemplify, teach and do research with a focus on race and ethnic studies programs.

“Apparently, my colleague had assumed that because I am Black, I must be an expert on the African diaspora,” wrote Tyler Austin Harper, a former environmental studies professor at Bates College, in an August 2026 article in The Atlantic, which detailed his decision to leave his tenure-track position.

“The school’s culture encouraged us to see professors of color as vehicles for achieving the college’s diversity goals. The inescapable conclusion I arrived at was that I had been hired to be visibly Black first and a scholar second, if at all,” Harper wrote.
Other faculty of color have reported feeling like they and their scholarship are undervalued by their schools and peers.
Some faculty of color also report that scholarship focusing on marginalized populations or social problems is treated as less rigorous or less central to their disciplines.
Faculty of color across American colleges and universities face other challenges, including feeling isolated or like they are being watched.
Some faculty of color also report feeling like they should mentor students of color. This work can add to their workloads and, they say, sometimes come at a cost to their own careers.
Some research has found racial disparities in tenure and promotion outcomes, although those disparities vary considerably by discipline, school, gender and racial or ethnic group.
LGBTQ+ faculty of color, in particular, also report feeling isolated or intimidated, and experiencing delayed tenure or other promotion opportunities.
A diverse faculty benefits everyone
Having diverse faculty can benefit students and universities in several ways.
Research has linked greater faculty diversity to a range of positive outcomes for students, including student retention and college completion, particularly for Black and Hispanic students.
Exposure to professors with different backgrounds and perspectives can broaden students’ educational experiences.
Having a diverse faculty at universities can also strengthen academic research.
Researchers’ backgrounds can influence the questions they ask, the populations they study and how participants respond to them.
More diverse research teams can also bring different experiences and perspectives to the design and interpretation of research.

Research teams and study populations that lack diversity can overlook important perspectives and produce findings that are less applicable to broader populations. Conversely, more diverse teams can bring a wider range of perspectives and approaches to research.
I believe that continuing to make university faculty ranks more diverse is essential for higher education.

This is not simply a matter of making professors more closely resemble the students they teach. It is about broadening the perspectives represented in classrooms and research, and ensuring that universities draw on the widest possible pool of scholars and ideas.

articles.title: Students from military families are often misunderstood in US public schools – a retired military officer and behavioral health expert explains what schools can do
articles.author: Nikki R Wooten, Associate Professor of Social Work, University of South Carolina
paras: Over 1.4 million children had a parent or caregiver who served in the U.S. armed forces in 2024.
Among active-duty families, 2.4% of military children had both parents serving in the military. Another 4% lived in single-parent households.

More than 90% of these children attend U.S. public schools. Over 67,000 attend Department of Defense schools located in the U.S. and foreign countries. Military-connected students have a unique set of experiences and academic and emotional needs, including support with school transitions and developing a sense of belonging at their new school.
Because only 6% of Americans have served in the U.S. military, some educators may not understand the experiences of military children and the challenges of military life.
As a retired U.S. Army lieutenant colonel and military behavioral health expert, I think there are a few key ways that school districts can better support these students through school transitions.
Some strategies include identifying military-connected students during enrollment and training educators about military life.
Benefits and drawbacks of military life
The military lifestyle creates both unique opportunities and challenges for children and teenagers whose parents are military service members.

Military children often travel and have opportunities to live in multiple cities across the U.S. and other countries. They are also exposed to different cultures, new traditions and opportunities to learn foreign languages.

These children are resilient and adaptable. They may also display increased independence, personal growth and pride because of their parent’s military service. Many are thriving in school because of these traits.
Military children are also twice as likely to serve in the military as their civilian peers.
But military life can also be stressful for children.

Many children with parents in the military move frequently. They often live in more cities and attend more schools than their civilian peers – an average of two schools during high school, and for most, six to nine different schools between kindergarten and 12th grade.
They experience their parent being away from home for various periods of time, ranging from a few weeks at a time to a year or more.
They also fear that their parent might be hurt or killed while serving in the military.

As a result, military children and teenagers may experience social withdrawal, angry outbursts and mental health problems, including depression and anxiety. These challenges might also cause them to miss school, struggle to complete school assignments and have difficulty making new friends.

Recent research found that military-connected students were more likely to be disengaged in school and repeat a grade than their civilian peers. Other studies found that multiple parental deployments and longer parental separations affected children negatively. Examples include greater family stress and behavioral problems.

Children’s responses to military life vary, depending on how old they are and their level of maturity. Children 5 and younger often have limited language skills to express their feelings. As a result, they may act out behaviorally in response to changes in caregivers and daily routines.
Elementary school students may have tantrums, be clingy, have toileting accidents, engage in uncontrollable crying or become less talkative as a result of changes in schools, homes and caregivers.
Middle school students and preteens, ages 8 to 13, are likely aware of how their lives are different from their civilian peers.

These students may have experienced multiple moves and attended multiple schools over their relatively short lives. They may respond to changes in schools and household routines with angry outbursts, irritability, anxiety and social withdrawal.
They may also have fluctuating grades, peer conflict, problems completing their homework and disciplinary problems at school.
Boys and girls may express their stress differently. Boys may exhibit more anger and aggression, whereas girls might demonstrate sadness, depression and self-harm.
Military adolescents and high school students, typically 14-18, have heightened risk for anxiety, depression and suicide due to military-related stressors, especially during parental deployments.

They may experience mood changes, anger and social withdrawal. They may also disengage from school activities, perform poorly in school and choose to skip classes. Many are also high achievers despite the challenges of military life.
Military adolescents are also at risk for substance use.
My prior research from 2019 found that military adolescents had frequent emergency department visits and hospitalizations for substance use problems during the Afghanistan and Iraq wars.
How schools can support military-connected students
Military-connected students transitioning to a new school often need help early in the process to ensure they have adjusted well to their new school.

As a licensed clinical social worker and former child therapist for military children, I think brief check-ins with a school counselor or social worker are necessary to identify concerns early. These check-ins can help avoid behavioral or academic difficulties and prevent a problem from becoming worse.
U.S. public schools are required to identify students with an active duty military parent, typically by asking about military affiliation during enrollment.
Some school districts also include children of veterans and those with parents in the National Guard and Reserves in these records.
Research has consistently shown that the impact of military life continues after parents leave military service.
An estimated 2.3 million children under 18 reside with a veteran who is disabled. These children often assume caregiving responsibilities for siblings and their veteran parent.
Identifying schools that support military-connected students

State education departments can give schools a Purple Star School designation, indicating that the school is committed to assisting with the academic, social and emotional needs of military-connected students. These schools maintain a list of military students, help students with school transitions and train school personnel about the challenges of military life.
Currently, there are over 4,100 Purple Star Schools in 44 states across the U.S.

The proportion of military-connected students in U.S. public schools depends on the military and veteran population of each state and school district, as well as the geographical location of military installations.
Texas, California, Florida, North Carolina, Georgia, South Carolina and Virginia rank among the 10 states with the most military families that have children attending public schools.

Schools can help military-connected children and their families by creating a welcoming school climate, maintaining open communication with students and parents, and developing student groups and peer-support programs.

Frequent school guidance counselor, nurse or social worker visits may also be needed. High schools can develop peer-mentoring programs and suicide prevention, mental health awareness and anti-stigma campaigns.
I think it is also important for schools not to rush to identify behaviors as a disciplinary problem when family stress is the root cause.

Although military-connected students face unique challenges to success in school, I think schools should intervene early and often to meet their needs. Helping these students ensures every child has an equal chance to succeed in school.

Nikki R. Wooten, PhD, LISW-CP previously received research funding from the National Institute on Drug Abuse. Dr. Wooten retired as a lieutenant colonel from the U. S. Army after over 33 years of military service. articles.title: AI can help with academic research but doesn’t always get it right – here are some tips to check the information you receive
articles.author: Allison Faix, Librarian and Instruction Coordinator, Coastal Carolina University
paras: Almost 25% of adults in the United States are using artificial intelligence chatbots on a daily basis, a 2026 Pew Research Center study found.
At the same time, another recent study found that 48% of the information that popular free chatbots gave in response to questions about the news contained errors.
As librarians, we know that if students are using AI chatbots to help with their academic research, they shouldn’t assume that the information they’re given is accurate.
Not all AI is the same. Here are four steps we recommend to question information AI generates, including by checking the original source and considering issues that aren’t always easy to spot.
First, we think it makes sense to spend time choosing the right AI tool for the task at hand.

AI tools – be it ExLibris’ Primo Research Assistant, Research Solutions’ Scite, Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT – are trained with various datasets and use different algorithms to generate results. They should not be used interchangeably.
Some tools might be better or worse at answering specific kinds of questions, and the types of answers they generate can vary.
People might choose ChatGPT, for example, at the beginning of their research process, because it can provide overviews and summaries to help with understanding concepts.
In subsequent stages, they might choose a tool such as Primo Research Assistant or Scopus AI, which can help find and examine peer-reviewed research that has been vetted by academics.

Students conducting academic research could also see whether their library subscribes to an artificial intelligence tool like LeapSpace or Concensus, which draw their data from peer-reviewed, scholarly research.
Using these specific AI tools doesn’t eliminate the need to evaluate their answers, but it provides more certainty that the data has gone through a review process.

Tools such as Anthropic’s Claude, meanwhile, may also draw from academic research, but to what extent is unclear. According to Anthropic, Claude states that it is trained on a proprietary mix of publicly available information from online sources, public and private datasets, user data and synthetic data generated by other models.
Finally, it can be helpful to read librarians’ reviews about AI tools to help select the best fit. People can also take a simple online test such as ROBOT to help them consider which tool to use.
Second, asking follow-up questions is an important part of evaluating the answers AI tools generate. Even if the answer an AI tool gives sounds good, it is useful to take time to learn more about it.

Checking one’s own emotions is also important, because AI chatbots have been known to flatter users by giving answers based on the user’s own biases, or what the user wants to hear, rather than just facts.

Ask the AI to tell you where it got the information, how confident it is that the answer is correct and what might be missing. Ask the AI why it believes the answer is correct, or ask it to explain how it came up with an answer.

It’s helpful to also make sure your prompt is phrased in a neutral way. For example, asking “What does psychological research say about social media and anxiety?” rather than “Tell me why social media causes anxiety” may produce different responses.
Third, it is useful to trace any claims the AI chatbot makes to their original sources.
Students may be familiar with using the SIFT process to evaluate websites. This process asks people to stop, investigate the source, find better coverage and trace claims to their original source.
Start by asking the chatbot to cite its sources, if it did not do that already.

Then, go to each source and read enough to figure out whether the AI is using the information in the right context. Also, look into who authored the source and whether they have expertise in the topic. If the AI won’t cite the sources it used, or if the sources it cites don’t include the information it said they did, pull out any claims it is making and do further research.

Can you find other, credible sources that back up what the AI is saying, using Google or a library database? Can you figure out where the AI may have gotten the information and whether that source is credible?
If this seems like a lot of work, you could always go directly to library databases instead of using AI tools.
4. Not all issues are easy to spot
Fourth, there are other, less visible issues that can play out when using AI tools.
For example, it might not always be easy to tell whether an AI tool is missing important perspectives or is giving biased information.

Remember that you, not the AI tool, are the researcher. It might be easy to rely on an AI tool to generate a summary of important sources, but deciding for yourself what sources to use helps you learn about a topic more deeply.

Research shows that most AI tools focus on sources such as websites, internet forums and other online content that is freely available and written in English. Consider what expert knowledge might be missing from AI datasets and seek out those viewpoints when needed.
Last, remember that you need to cite the AI tool you used if you are quoting or paraphrasing text generated by it in your work, just as you would cite any other source.
Artificial intelligence is changing fast. As librarians, we think it is important to continually evaluate whether the tools you are using are still working for you.
These tips are a good place to start to help sharpen your evaluation skills.
